02 · The problem

Gate-in was slow. But the bigger problem was trust.

Figures below describe the manual baseline documented in the concept brief — representative of terminal gate operations, not client measurements.

01

Transcription under glare

An 11-character ISO 6346 code copied by hand off a moving truck. One wrong digit corrupts the chain of custody.

02

Queues compound

Every slow manual inspection multiplies across the trucks behind it — peak waits stretch to 18–47 minutes per lane.

03

Damage is deniable

Without time-stamped evidence at entry, every cut seal becomes a liability argument between yard, carrier and shipping line.

04

Trust without surrender

AI can read and flag in seconds — but an inspection is a legal record. Automation must never erase the accountable human.

04 · Design principles

Three rules explain the whole system

P1
AI proposes. Humans decide.

The model never touches the gatepass — evidence flows to an accountable person, and high severity adds a second signature.

P2
Every decision needs evidence.

Photos, per-character reads, confidence scores, and the case for and against each finding — recorded append-only.

P3
Failure is part of the primary experience.

Ten edge states aren't error pages; they're the product working under real conditions.

Decisions at a glance

Challenge Decision Why
AI confidence alone isn't trustworthy Show evidence + confidence, for and against Makes the AI inspectable, not just believable
Gloved operators mis-tap Undo on every judgment until submission An accidental tap never becomes a record
Supervisors get delayed Show ETA + escalation path Reduces uncertainty at the flow's low point
Cameras fail outdoors Manual fallback with preserved timestamps Workflow continuity survives the outage
Findings get disputed Append-only history, named decisions Disagreement preserves accountability

The common cost of these calls: every safeguard adds a tap. I accepted a slower single-truck ceiling to protect record integrity — the six-minute budget absorbs it.

REJECTED

Verdict-first layout. Leading with the AI's conclusion read as a decision already made — evidence became decoration.

REJECTED

Auto-approval above a threshold. Faster on paper; unownable when the 6% case reaches a courtroom.

REJECTED

Edge states as modals. Overlays die on restart; a camera outage must survive navigation, so failures became sibling screens.

05 · Information architecture & hand-offs

A corridor, not a maze

I kept Gate-In deliberately linear: an operator mid-inspection can move forward, retry, or back out one level, never sideways into another truck's context. Free navigation lost; cross-truck mistakes gone. Edge states are siblings of their happy-path screen, not detours.

The corridor starts before the first truck

Two entry screens run before Lane Check-In. The operator declares where they are and which shift they're on — so every decision made afterwards is already attributed to a named person, in a named zone, on a named shift.

Accountability begins at sign-inZone and shift are captured before any inspection — the audit trail starts here, not at the gate.
One choice per screenTerminal zone is the only decision. No settings, no menus — the linear corridor begins immediately.
Context carries forwardThe selected zone scopes which lanes appear on the next screen — Lane Check-In is never a global list.

Five actors, four transitions — each carrying evidence, an expected response window, and preserved state.

Driver→AI→Operator→Supervisor→Gatepass→Yard control

AI proposes. Humans decide. Every decision leaves evidence.

06 · Identification & inspection
The AI shouldn't simply say "Verified"

A single green "Verified" label hides too much information. I broke every AI claim into parts an operator can check in seconds, then attributed the confirmed record to a person. The cost: a busier screen than a clean checkmark. I took that trade, because a checkmark is unfalsifiable.

Live evidenceThe camera frame stays visible while the AI reads — the operator sees what the model sees. Per-character OCRMSKU-774521 in inspectable boxes; the ISO 6346 check digit renders green when valid. Confidence, not certainty97% is a claim to examine — never silently accepted. Absence ≠ blockedNo pre-advice downgrades to a notice; plate + seal carry forward.

Six surfaces, argued with evidence

The AI photographs and analyses every surface, then presents findings as evidence — thumbnails for what passed, severity and photos for what didn't. Nothing is summarised into a verdict.

07 · Human judgment
The AI argues. The human decides.

94% confidence ≠ automatic approval. Because of that principle, I changed the UI in four specific ways — evidence first, severity named, counter-evidence listed, every decision reversible:

01 02 03 04
  1. 01Evidence before verdict

    The photograph leads. The operator sees what the camera saw before reading any conclusion — a swipeable set, not a single framed shot.

  2. 02Severity is named, not colour-coded

    "High severity" in words next to the finding, so urgency survives sunlight, glare and colour-blindness.

  3. 03The argument, for and against

    Three observations that support the finding, two that don't — plus the confidence ring. Counter-evidence is what makes the number trustworthy.

  4. 04The decision stays human

    Reject and Confirm carry equal weight, both reversible until submission. The AI never reaches the gatepass.

Anatomy of a machine claim

The AI doesn’t replace the operator. It removes the guesswork — and shows its work.

Every AI claim in Gate-In must carry four things before a human is asked to act on it. Nothing in the system may propose a finding without all four.

01 · What it saw
Seal damageHigh severityRear panel · photographed
02 · How sure
94%Confidence, shown — not hidden behind a verdict
03 · The argument, both ways
Seal wire is broken
Pattern not matched
Seal geometry mismatch
Seal ID readable
OCR matched records
04 · Who decides
RejectConfirm issue Equal weight · both reversible until submission

The model never writes to the gatepass. A named person does.

08 · Supervisor approval

The hardest moment isn't inspection.
It's waiting for approval.

The operator has done everything right and control passes to someone else. That loss of agency is the emotional low point of the journey, so I gave it the most design attention.

"Stays on record — not an override"The supervisor's push-back is a re-work request in his own words; the operator's confirmation survives it.
Expectation-set waitingEst. response time, the supervisor's note, and an explicit promise: escalation keeps your inspection intact.
Credit on approval"Good catch on the seal — documented and escalated." Closure with recognition, not just clearance.
09 · Failure states

Designed for bad days

Each one follows the same contract: state what changed, protect completed work, name the next action.

10of 24

screens exist for things going wrong — camera faults, failed reads, missing records, delayed approvals. They were designed alongside the happy path, not after it.

The operating principle

Automation accelerates the corridor.
It never shortens the chain of accountability.

AI appears twice in the flow — and both times it hands work to a human, never to the gatepass

10 · Design system

One language for AI, status and urgency

The one strict rule
Purple appears only when a machine is judging.

82 tokens. Sunlight-legible neutrals, one working amber, status colours that belong to content and never to chrome — so when purple shows up, it can only mean one thing.

Three surfaces, one rule. Everywhere else — buttons, chrome, status, severity — purple is forbidden.

11 · Outcome / success criteria

Success targets — and what the concept delivers

The figures below are success targets the design was built against — not measured outcomes. The qualitative outcomes describe what the designed system does.

Concept validation — the honest position: this is a self-initiated concept — the design was reviewed against the documented manual process, operational requirements, and workflow constraints; there was no client and no primary user testing in this phase. Because this is a concept exploration rather than an implemented system, the next step would be validating the prototype with operators in real gate conditions. What I would test: can operators verify AI identification quickly · do confidence + evidence create enough trust · can a failed scan be recovered without losing progress · can supervisors see why a truck is waiting · does the corridor actually reduce cognitive load. Nothing below is claimed as measured.

Scope designed: 24 screens + 3 supporting overlays · 2 additional authentication states planned.

The goal wasn't to automate the gate. It was to make the gate smarter — AI where it accelerates work, people accountable for the decisions that matter.

12 · Key takeaways

Three things this project taught me

01
Automation needs an audience, not just accuracy.

94% confidence is meaningless unless the operator can see why — and disagree.

02
The low point wasn't a failure state.

It was the approval hold, where the operator loses agency. That screen needed expectation-setting, not a spinner.

03
Design the outage before the demo.

Ten of twenty-four screens exist for bad days. Retrofitting them would have produced a different architecture.
